title: Scope and Lifetimes
story: Variables have a lifespan — they're born at declaration and die at the end of their scope. Borrows must always die before the values they reference.
why: Understanding scope and lifetimes is essential for writing code that compiles — borrows cannot outlive the data they point to.
analogy: Scope is like a room. Variables live inside the room. When you leave the room, everything inside is cleaned up. You can't reference something in a room you've already left.
try_it: Try declaring a borrow in an inner scope and using it in the outer scope. The compiler will tell you the borrow doesn't live long enough.
tips: Values are dropped at the end of their scope, in reverse order of declaration
Borrows must ALWAYS end before the owned value they reference
Use nested scopes { } to limit how long borrows live
Non-lexical lifetimes mean borrows end at last use, not scope end
common_mistakes: Returning a reference to a local variable — the local is destroyed on return
Holding a borrow across a scope boundary where the owner is dropped
Assuming borrows live until the end of scope — they end at last use
